newsitem.title: INDIA: Santa comes early for rallying Indian shares.
newsitem.headline: Santa comes early for rallying Indian shares.

text.p: Lured by attractive valuations and hopes of a turnaround, fund managers are driving Indian shares higher after a year spent mostly counting losses, analysts said on Wednesday.

In afternoon trade on Wednesday, the 30-share benchmark index of the Bombay Stock Exchange was up 28.83 points, or 0.96 percent, at 3,012.85 -- about 11 percent higher than the three-year low of 2,713.12 reached on December 4.
"Santa has come to town," said Ramesh Damani, a top member-broker at the BSE. "The market is celebrating an early Christmas."
He attributed the rally to the return of big local and foreign institutional investors.

Analysts see the depressed market bottoming out after discounting a series of negative factors, such as an economic slowdown, poor first-half company results and the coalition government's inability to push through liberalisation measures.
They believe the market has fallen enough to make share valuations attractive.
"The selling frenzy in the recent past was the result of all-round pessimism ...with valuations counting for little," said Ramnath Iyer, strategist at Peregrine Capital.

Local traders said expectations of higher allocations flowing into India in January and the government's resolve to tackle the problems affecting the stock market were other factors pushing shares higher.
Sunil Kothari at brokerage Nagindas Kothari said he expected the recovery to carry on until the end of February when the Indian government traditionally presents its annual budget.
Peregrine said it was overweight in oil refining, banking, consumer and capital goods scrips. It recommended investors to go underweight in steel, cement and financial instruments.

"We believe the sharp decline in the earnings gap trend in recent months...will reverse soon to reflect the comparatively attractive yields on equities -- and this provides an excellent signal to increase weightings in the Indian market," Iyer said in a report.

"The underperformance of India compared to Asian and other emerging markets in 1996 means that comparative valuations will not be a factor holding back India's attractiveness from an international perspective," he said.
